per-million-what.title: Per Million What
per-million-what.closing: A crash count means nothing until it is set against the traffic that was exposed. Annualize the daily count so the periods match, scale to a million so the answer is readable, and carry the length as well when it is a stretch of road rather than a junction. A busier place with more crashes can be the safer one.

brief.title: Crashes over the traffic that was exposed
steps: A count alone ranks nothing
A busy junction has more crashes than a quiet one simply because more cars go through it. To compare two places you have to divide by how much traffic was exposed.
Build the bottom of the fraction
Traffic is usually given per DAY, so multiply by 365 to get a year, matching a year of crashes. Divide by the daily count instead and you get thousands, claiming more crashes than vehicles.
The million is just for reading
Rates come out as tiny decimals, so the answer is quoted per million vehicles. That is all the ten to the sixth is doing.
Junction or stretch of road
At a junction the exposure is vehicles ENTERING. Along a road it is vehicle MILES, because a car on three miles of highway is exposed three times as long.

right.caption: twenty crashes, but far more traffic passed through

rounds.subject: why a count is not enough
rounds.asked: One intersection has 12 crashes a year and another has 20. Which is more dangerous?
options: The one with 20, obviously
The one with 12, since fewer crashes means a worse road
It cannot be said until each count is set against the traffic that went through
Neither: crash counts are not comparable at all
rounds.why: You cannot tell yet. A crossroads carrying thirty thousand vehicles a day has far more chances to produce a crash than one carrying eight thousand. Dividing by the traffic is what makes two places comparable, and that division is the whole of this calculation.

rounds.subject: building the denominator
rounds.asked: The count here is 8,000 vehicles a DAY and the crashes are counted over a YEAR. What goes underneath?
options: 8,000, the daily count
8,000 times 365, the vehicles that entered in the year
8,000 divided by 365
365 on its own
rounds.why: The whole year of traffic, 2.92 million vehicles. The periods have to match: a year of crashes over a year of traffic. Dividing by the daily count instead gives 1,500 per million, which is the lesson's wrong answer and is absurd on its face, since it would mean more crashes than vehicles.

rounds.subject: why a million
rounds.asked: The formula multiplies by a million. What would happen without it?
options: The answer would be four millionths of a crash per vehicle, a number nobody can hold in their head
Nothing: it cancels
The units would change to crashes a day
The answer would be a hundred times too big
rounds.why: You would be quoting crashes per vehicle, which for any real intersection is a few millionths. Scaling to a million entering vehicles puts the answer in the range of ones and tens, where engineers can compare places at a glance.

rounds.subject: more crashes, better road
rounds.asked: This intersection has 20 crashes a year on 30,000 vehicles a day. How does its rate compare with the 12 crashes on 8,000 a day?
options: Worse: more crashes
Better: nearly four times the traffic for under twice the crashes
The same
It cannot be compared at all
rounds.why: Better, and it is not close: about 1.8 per million entering against 4.1. This is exactly why rates exist. A programme that ranked sites by raw counts would spend its money at the busiest places rather than the most dangerous ones.

rounds.subject: a length of road instead
rounds.asked: Now the crashes are on three miles of highway rather than at one intersection. What changes in the denominator?
options: Nothing changes
The days come out of it
The length joins it: the exposure is vehicle MILES, not vehicles
The crashes are divided by three
rounds.why: The length joins in, because a vehicle on a three mile stretch is exposed three times as long as one crossing a single intersection. So a segment rate is per million vehicle miles and an intersection rate is per million entering vehicles, and the two are not interchangeable.

rounds.subject: which rate belongs where
rounds.asked: A city wants to rank its worst signalized junctions. Which rate should it use?
options: Per million vehicle miles, since that is the more precise measure
Per million entering vehicles, because a junction is a place rather than a length
Either: they give the same ranking
Neither: use the raw count
rounds.why: Entering vehicles, because a junction has no meaningful length. Mixing the two measures makes a list that cannot be read: the numbers are in different units and a low figure in one is not comparable with a low figure in the other.

tap-the-voids.title: Tap the Voids
tap-the-voids.closing: Three bands and a bracket. Air voids are the air over the WHOLE specimen. VMA is the air and the binder together, the whole space between the stones. VFA is the binder as a share of that bracket, never of the whole mix. And the term the VMA formula subtracts is the stone, which is why it comes out near eighty six and the VMA near fourteen.
tap-the-voids.note: one specimen by volume. the voids are drawn far bigger than they are, or nothing could be pointed at

brief.title: Three things in the mix, and what each share is of
steps: A road surface is three things
Compacted asphalt is stone, the black binder that glues it, and air. Every number on this page is one of those three as a share of something else. Getting the something else right is the whole skill.
Air voids: air against the WHOLE specimen
How far the compacted mix is from the same mix with no air left in it. That is what the two gravities give you, one measured with air and one without.
VMA: all the space between the stones
The air and the binder together, however that space happens to be filled. It is what is left once you take the stone volume away from a hundred.
VFA: the binder as a share of THAT space
Not of the whole mix. Design sits near four percent air, with enough room between the stones to carry a proper film of binder around every one.
spoken: how far the compacted mix falls short of the airless one
a hundred, less the share that is stone
the binder as a percent of the space between the stones

picture.caption: a compacted specimen by volume: stone, then binder, then air. the bracket is the space between the stones

rounds.subject: a mix at the design point
rounds.asked: Tap the part that the air void percentage measures.
rounds.why: The air, as a share of the WHOLE specimen. That is what the formula with the two gravities gives you: how far the compacted mix is from the same mix with no air in it at all. Four percent is where Superpave aims, which is this specimen exactly.

rounds.subject: the space between the stones
rounds.asked: Tap what the voids in the mineral aggregate measure.
rounds.why: The bracket: air and binder together, which is all the space between the stones however it is filled. That is why the hierarchy in the lesson reads VMA equals air plus the binder voids, and why VMA is always the bigger of the two numbers.

rounds.subject: what VFA is a share of
rounds.asked: Voids filled with asphalt is the binder as a share of something. Tap the something.
rounds.why: The VMA, not the whole specimen. VFA asks how much of the space between the stones the binder has taken: eleven parts out of fifteen here, so about 73 percent. Dividing the binder by the whole mix instead gives 11, which is why the lesson names that as a wrong answer.

rounds.subject: the theoretical maximum
rounds.asked: Tap the part that the theoretical maximum specific gravity assumes is not there.
rounds.why: The air. That gravity is the same aggregate and the same binder with the air squeezed out, which is why it is always the LARGER of the two: more mass in less volume. If your air voids come out negative, you have the two the wrong way round.

rounds.subject: a thin film around every stone
rounds.asked: This mix looks dry and the film around each stone is too thin. Tap the part there is too little of.
rounds.why: The binder, which is the part VFA counts. With the stones packed this tightly the VMA is only twelve percent, and once the air has taken its share there is very little room left for asphalt. That is why VMA is specified as a minimum: not for its own sake, but because a mix with nowhere to put binder gets a film too thin to last, and it oxidizes and cracks whatever the air voids say.

rounds.subject: what the long term looks like
rounds.asked: The VMA formula subtracts one term from a hundred. Tap the part that term measures.
rounds.why: The stone itself. The bulk gravity times the aggregate share over the aggregate gravity is the volume the aggregate occupies, and whatever is not stone is VMA. Reporting that subtracted term as the answer gives 86 percent, which is the other wrong answer the lesson names, and it should look obviously wrong: a compacted mix is not 86 percent void.

in-what-order.title: In What Order
in-what-order.closing: Closest party first, then up the chain, and the authority when the chain runs out. The exception is imminent danger, which stops the work before anything else happens. And one action on every board is one nobody should take.
in-what-order.hint: one of the four is not taken at all

brief.title: Up the ladder, one rung at a time
brief.handbook: Handbook pp. 4-5, Model Rules A.3, A.8
steps: Start with the person
You spot a problem in someone's work. First tell that person. They may simply not have seen it, and most problems end right here.
Then the firm
If nothing changes, go to the firm. It has the standing and the duty to fix its own work.
Then the board
Only when the rungs below have been tried and nothing moved do you go to the authority or the board. Skipping a rung turns a fixable error into an argument about you.
The one exception
When people are about to be hurt, you stop the work first and explain afterwards. Danger right now does not wait for the ladder.
spoken: the person, then the firm, then the board, in that order
object in writing, tell your employer, then the authority
if someone is about to be hurt, stop first and go up the ladder after

picture.caption: one rung at a time: the person, then the firm, then the board. Skipping one is the mistake

rounds.scenario: A colleague made a material error in a soil bearing capacity report for a school building, and it has already gone to the client.
actions: Report it to the licensing board
Raise it with the colleague directly
Post an anonymous warning on a public forum
Take it to the firm's management
rounds.never: A public forum reaches everyone except the people who can fix it, and it is not a channel the rules recognize.
rounds.why: The colleague first, because they may simply not have seen it. Then the firm, which has both the standing and the obligation to correct its own work. The board is what is left when neither acts.

rounds.scenario: The client wants a cheaper mix than the code allows for a parking garage, and the plans are with you for your seal.
actions: Refuse to seal the plans
Seal the plans with a disclaimer limiting your liability
Notify the building authority if the client proceeds anyway
Tell the client the design has to meet code
rounds.never: A disclaimer moves paperwork around. It does not move concrete, and the garage is no safer for having one.
rounds.why: Say it before you refuse, because the client may not know. Refuse when they insist, because a seal is a statement you would be making. And the authority hears about it only if the work goes ahead.

rounds.scenario: You are on the selection committee for a highway bridge, and a firm owned by a close friend has bid for it.
actions: Tell the committee about the friendship
Let the remaining members score the bids
Step out of this selection
Recommend the firm, since it is well qualified
rounds.never: Recommending them is the thing the rule exists to prevent, and the firm being good at its job is not a defense.
rounds.why: Disclose before you recuse, or the recusal is a gap in the record that nobody can read. Then step out of this decision only, and let the committee get on with it without you.

rounds.scenario: You are on site and the scaffold on the east elevation is visibly unbraced. Crews go up at seven tomorrow morning.
actions: Raise it at the weekly safety meeting
Stop the work on that elevation now
Notify the authority if it is not corrected
Tell the site superintendent
rounds.never: The weekly meeting is after the crews go up. A schedule is not a reason and a calendar is not a channel.
rounds.why: Imminent danger inverts the ladder. You stop it first and explain afterwards, because the chain of command is a way of getting things fixed and not a reason to let somebody fall.

rounds.scenario: You find an error in a drawing you sealed. The building is already under construction.
actions: Issue a corrected drawing
Notify the building authority if the work has passed that stage
Tell your employer immediately
Correct it quietly on the next revision
rounds.never: A quiet correction is a bet that nobody built to the old sheet, and it is not yours to make on somebody else's behalf.
rounds.why: The ladder does not change because the error is yours. Your employer first, then the corrected sheet so there is something to build to, then the authority if the wrong thing is already standing.

rounds.scenario: The client has overruled your judgment on a retaining wall and you believe the design as instructed endangers the public.
actions: Notify the building authority
Resign from the job and say nothing
Put your objection to the client in writing
Notify your employer
rounds.never: Walking away leaves the wall exactly where it was and takes the one person who understood the problem off the project.
rounds.why: In writing first, so the objection exists somewhere other than a conversation. Then your employer, who carries the firm's share of this. Then the authority, which is the point of the rule.
